scenes.text: [warmly, with quiet wonder] A person types a single sentence describing the song they imagine, and a minute later a complete piece arrives, with a singer, instruments and a chorus that was never written by anyone. [pause] [curious] No musician was in the room, so what is the machine actually doing, and how can it produce something that sounds composed?

[calmly, explanatory] The first idea is to treat sound as language. A raw recording is far too detailed to predict directly, so an audio codec compresses it into a long sequence of small discrete units called tokens, much as a sentence is made of words. [pause] Once music is a sequence of tokens, it becomes something a language model knows how to handle.

[steady, patient, building admiration] The model is trained on a vast collection of recordings, each paired with a description, and its task is always the same: given the tokens so far, predict the next one. [pause] By doing this BILLIONS of times it absorbs how rhythm holds together, how a chord tends to follow another, and how a voice shapes a word, without being handed any rules of music theory.

[engaged, with quiet momentum] Your prompt is the steering. The description of style is converted into numbers that guide every prediction, while lyrics, which can be written by a separate language model, tell the singer which syllables to place and when. [pause] The song is then generated one token after another, each choice shaped by everything that came before it and by what you asked for.

[reflective, with a quiet reveal] Tokens are only a code, so a decoder converts them back into an audible waveform, rebuilding the detail that the compression had set aside. [pause] This is why the result can feel so polished, and also why the same prompt gives a DIFFERENT song each time, because every prediction is a weighted draw among many plausible continuations.
[warmly, satisfied, slowing down] A sentence, a model that has learned how music tends to unfold, and a decoder that turns that learning back into sound.
